newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU treaty allows for tougher environment rules.
newsitem.headline: EU treaty allows for tougher environment rules.

text.p: European Union member states will be able to introduce stricter environmental legislation on their own under language incorporated in the bloc's new Treaty of Amsterdam.
EU leaders at a summit agreed on treaty rules making it possible for members to maintain and introduce tougher environmental provisions, provided they did not amount to trade protectionism.

Denmark, in particular, pushed hard in the final stages of Tuesday's late-night negotiations to change the wording of the new text, making it more difficult for the European Commission to block a country from introducing national environmental provisions.
"This is a big step forward," Swedish Foreign Minister Lena Hjelm-Wallen told reporters late on Tuesday.
Although there was no final text of the Amsterdam Treaty available on Wednesday, a Nordic official said there did not appear to have been any last-minute changes on that issue.
"This is how Sweden and Denmark see it."

The issue is controversial because stricter environmental rules in one member state could run counter to the bloc's single market, in which goods are supposed to move across internal borders without restrictions.
Fearing new barriers to trade, industry seems certain to criticise the idea.
But the Nordics argued that the bloc must be seen as giving priority to issues which matter for ordinary people, such as jobs and the environment.
This also reflects the fact that large parts of their populations are at best euro-sceptical.
The text on the environment may go down well with the public and help secure approval of the treaty in a referendum that Denmark will hold on the revised treaty.

Under the treaty text, a member state which finds it necessary to introduce national rules based on new scientific evidence relating to the protection of the environment must first notify the European Commission.
The Brussels-based EU executive must then approve or reject the planned provisions within six months.

Following Nordic pressure, the new rules are approved if the Commission has not taken a decision on the issue within six months. The original proposal from the Dutch EU presidency had it the other way around.
However, the text also states that the stricter environmental rules must not constitute a disguised restriction on trade in the EU.
